messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Keanu has spent the last fifteen years of his life in a state of controlled calm, a professional necessity for an airline pilot responsible for hundreds of lives. But for the past eight months, that control has felt like a thin sheet of ice over a churning, violent sea. The trouble began on a hot August night. He was in the passenger seat of his friend’s car when the flashing lights appeared behind them. What followed was a blur of mistaken identity, of being yanked from the car and thrown face-down onto the hot, gritty asphalt. The officers were shouting, their faces inches from his, their physical presence an overwhelming, suffocating weight. Pinned in the back of the squad car, the combination of cheap air freshener, vinyl seats, and sheer terror brought on a wave of nausea so intense he thought he would be sick. The short drive to the station felt like an eternity of helplessness, trapped with the very people who had just brutalized him.

Since that night, the world has become a landscape of hidden threats. At work, the once-routine sounds of the aircraft are now sources of alarm; the click of a galley latch or the thud of a bag in an overhead bin causes him to jolt in his seat, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has come to believe that any unexpected delay is a sign of impending catastrophe. During a recent pre-flight check, a fifteen-minute hold on the tarmac sent him into a spiral of dread, certain that maintenance had missed a critical engine flaw and they were all moments from disaster. He finds himself watching passengers in the terminal with a profound sense of suspicion. A stranger who walks too directly towards him can trigger a cold sweat, his mind instantly assessing them as a potential threat, a replay of the officers approaching the car.

The memory of the event itself is a paradox that lives in his mind. When it returns, it is not a recollection but a full-body reenactment. He can feel the rough texture of the pavement on his cheek and smell the exhaust fumes, the terror as raw and immediate as it was that night. These flashes are more vivid, more viscerally real, than the memory of his own wedding day or the birth of his daughter. Yet, at the same time, the story feels utterly impossible. That he, Keanu, a respected pilot, could be treated that way feels like a scene from a film, so extreme and unjust that it couldn't possibly have happened to him. This disconnect leaves him feeling untethered from his own life story.

The triggers have systematically dismantled his life. The nausea he felt in the police car has become a potent internal cue; any feeling of sickness, even from mild turbulence or something he ate, can plunge him back into that state of helpless fear. He can no longer tolerate being a passenger in a car. This became an impossible point of friction in his marriage. His ex-wife, Lena, could not understand why he would grip the dashboard in panic when she drove, or why he would refuse to let her take the wheel, and his inability to explain the terror eventually drove them apart. He now avoids crew shuttles, spending a small fortune on rental cars he can drive himself, isolating himself from his colleagues. The simple act of someone standing too close behind him in the security line feels like a physical assault, a violation of a boundary he can no longer defend.

Keanu has sought therapy because he is on the verge of losing the only part of his identity that still feels real: his wings. After his near-paralyzing panic during the tarmac delay, his first officer filed a report expressing concern for his fitness to fly. He is now on mandatory leave pending a psychological evaluation. What frightens him most is not the memory itself, but the terrifying certainty that he has been permanently broken, that the calm, competent man he once was is gone forever. He is here hoping to find a way to reclaim the cockpit of his own mind, to once again feel safe in the world and in his own skin.
